questions.stem: What makes a resource renewable?
options: It is typically replenished within years to decades
It can be recycled after it has been used at least once
It is found in every country in large amounts
It never runs out, however fast people use it
questions.explanation: Renewable resources, such as water, timber and fish, are replaced by natural processes on timescales of years to decades. They can still be depleted if used faster than they are replenished. Recycling applies to many non-renewable materials too.

questions.stem: Which of these is a harvestable renewable resource?
options: Iron ore from an open pit
Natural gas from a sedimentary basin
Gold from an alluvial deposit
Timber from a plantation forest
questions.explanation: A plantation can be regrown and harvested again within decades. Iron ore, natural gas and gold formed over geological time, so they are non-renewable.

questions.stem: A groundwater aquifer is refilled by rainfall at about 2 GL per year, but 5 GL per year is pumped out. How should this use be described?
options: Sustainable, as long as the pumping stays at a steady yearly rate
Unsustainable, because any use of groundwater is depletion
Unsustainable, because extraction exceeds the recharge rate
Sustainable, because groundwater is always a renewable resource
questions.explanation: A renewable resource is used sustainably only if it is used no faster than it is replenished. Taking 5 GL while only 2 GL is recharged lowers the water table year after year. Using up to about 2 GL a year could be sustained.

questions.stem: Why can a fish stock that is abundant and breeds quickly sustain a higher harvest rate than a rare, slow-breeding species?
options: Abundant species are never affected by habitat loss or pollution
Slow-breeding species are always protected from any harvesting
Rare species replace their numbers faster once they are harvested
Its losses are replaced faster, so more can be taken safely
questions.explanation: The sustainable rate of use depends on how much of the resource there is and how quickly it is replenished. A large, fast-breeding population replaces harvested individuals quickly; a small, slow-breeding one may take decades to recover from the same harvest.

questions.stem: Water from a large river is shared by several regions along its length. Why must sustainable use be assessed at the regional scale as well as locally?
options: Each town's local water use can never affect any other region
Rivers are replenished faster when more regions draw from them
Local use is always sustainable if each town has its own weir
Extraction upstream reduces the flow left for users downstream
questions.explanation: In a connected river system, water taken in one region is not available downstream, so the total extraction across the basin must be within what the system can supply. Each town's use may look small, but the combined effect can dry the lower river.

questions.stem: Which list contains only provisioning ecosystem services?
options: Fresh water, climate control and inspiration
Food, fresh water and pharmaceuticals
Food, pollination and soil formation
Carbon sequestration, timber and recreation
questions.explanation: Provisioning services are the products people take from ecosystems, such as food, water, timber and medicines. Soil formation is a supporting service, carbon sequestration and climate control are regulating services, and recreation and inspiration are cultural services.

questions.stem: Mangroves and forests take up carbon dioxide and store the carbon in their biomass. Which category of ecosystem service is this?
options: A harvestable resource
A regulating service
A provisioning service
A cultural service
questions.explanation: Carbon sequestration helps regulate the climate, so it is a regulating service. Provisioning services are products such as food and timber, and cultural services are non-material benefits such as aesthetics.

questions.stem: Under the categories of ecosystem services, which category includes soil formation and nutrient cycling?
options: Provisioning services
Cultural services
Harvestable services
Supporting services
questions.explanation: Supporting services, such as soil formation, nutrient and water cycling, and air and water purification, underpin the other services. They are not usually used directly but are needed to keep ecosystems producing food, water and other benefits.

questions.stem: People visit a national park to bushwalk, photograph the scenery and learn about its plants. Which category of ecosystem service does this represent?
options: Supporting services
Provisioning services
Cultural services
Regulating services
questions.explanation: Cultural services are the non-material benefits people get from ecosystems, including aesthetics, recreation and knowledge. Nothing is harvested and no physical process is being regulated, so the other categories do not fit.

questions.stem: A wetland upstream of a city is drained for housing. Afterwards, the river below shows more nutrients and sediment, and floods peak higher. Which ecosystem services were lost?
options: Recreation and scenic beauty only
Soil formation and pollination
Water purification and flood regulation
Food provision and timber supply only
questions.explanation: Wetlands filter sediment and nutrients from water and store floodwater, releasing it slowly. Losing them reduces water purification and flood regulation, so downstream water quality falls and flood peaks rise. Cultural services may also be lost, but they do not explain these data.

questions.stem: Renewable resources include harvestable resources and services. Which of these is a service rather than a harvestable resource?
options: Water pumped from a river
Timber cut from a plantation
Pollination of crops by insects
Fish caught by a coastal fishery
questions.explanation: Pollination is a process that ecosystems perform for people, so it is a service; it is usually classed as a regulating service. Fish, river water and timber are taken from ecosystems and used, so they are harvestable resources.

questions.stem: After years of heavy insecticide spraying in an orchard district, native bee and other pollinator numbers fall sharply. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Fruit yields fall, because a regulating service has been reduced
Fruit yields rise, because fewer insects compete for the nectar
Only cultural services are lost, so the harvest is unaffected
Soil formation stops at once, so the trees die within a season
questions.explanation: Many fruit crops depend on insects to carry pollen between flowers. Losing pollinators reduces this regulating service, so fewer flowers set fruit. This shows how human activity can push populations down and impact the ecosystem services people rely on.

questions.stem: Why is the cost-effective use of renewable energy limited, even though sunlight and wind are free?
options: Sunlight and wind energy cannot be turned into electricity at all
Renewable sources run out quickly once people start to use them heavily
Renewable energy can only ever be used at the place where it is collected
Technology to collect, store and transfer the energy is inefficient
questions.explanation: Solar panels and wind turbines convert only part of the incoming energy into electricity, storage loses some energy, and transmission over long distances loses more. Each loss raises the cost per unit of useful energy. The sources themselves are not used up.

questions.stem: A solar panel of area 1.7 m² receives 1000 W m⁻² of sunlight and converts 20% of it to electrical energy. What is its electrical power output?
questions.explanation: Incoming power = 1000 × 1.7 = 1700 W. Output = 20% × 1700 = 340 W. Taking 20% of 1000 W ignores the area, and 1700 W is the input, not the output. The remaining 80% becomes mostly heat.

questions.stem: Why do solar and wind farms often need energy storage, such as batteries or pumped hydro, to supply a steady electricity grid?
options: Their output is too steady to follow changes in demand
They only work when connected to a coal-fired station
Their output varies with the weather and time of day
They produce direct current that the grid cannot use
questions.explanation: Solar output falls to zero at night and drops under cloud, and wind output rises and falls with wind speed. Storage holds surplus energy for later use. Each storage step loses some energy, which adds to the cost.

questions.stem: Pumped hydro stores energy by pumping water uphill and later letting it flow down through turbines. Suppose 100 MWh is used to pump the water and 75 MWh is recovered. What does this show?
options: About a quarter of the energy is lost to friction and heat in the cycle
Energy is destroyed in storage, so pumped hydro breaks conservation of energy
The water gains extra energy on the way down, adding to the output
Storage is 133% efficient, because the output exceeds the input
questions.explanation: The efficiency is 75/100 = 75%. The missing 25 MWh is not destroyed: it becomes heat through friction and losses in pumps, turbines and pipes. Each energy transfer wastes some, so storage raises the cost of renewable energy.

questions.stem: A remote solar farm is built where sunlight is strong, but the city it supplies is 600 km away. Which factor reduces the energy that reaches the city?
options: The city's buildings blocking the sunlight reaching the farm
Energy lost as heat in the long transmission lines
Sunlight weakening as the electricity travels along the wires
Electricity running out once it passes a certain distance
questions.explanation: Current in transmission lines heats the wires, so some energy is lost over long distances; this is a transfer limit on renewable energy. The electricity does not 'run out' at a distance, and conditions at the city do not affect the sunlight at the farm.

questions.stem: Which is a natural process that can reduce the quality of fresh water in a river?
options: A blue-green algal bloom in warm, slow-flowing water
Discharge of treated sewage from a large city
Runoff of fertiliser from nearby farmland
Over-extraction of river water for irrigation
questions.explanation: Algal blooms, siltation and drought are natural processes that can lower water quality, although human activity often makes them worse. Sewage discharge, fertiliser runoff and over-extraction are human activities.

questions.stem: How does urbanisation tend to affect the water reaching streams in a catchment?
options: Lawns absorb all the rain, so streams stop flowing after storms
Hard surfaces increase fast runoff, carrying more pollutants to streams
Hard surfaces increase infiltration, so streams get cleaner groundwater
Buildings reduce rainfall, so streams receive less water each year
questions.explanation: Roofs, roads and car parks stop rain soaking into the soil, so more water runs off quickly into drains and streams. This raises flood peaks and carries oil, litter, metals and nutrients into waterways, while groundwater recharge falls.

questions.stem: In 1991 a blue-green algal bloom stretched for about 1000 km along the Barwon-Darling River in New South Wales. Which combination of conditions favours such blooms?
options: Low nutrient levels, cold water and fast, turbulent flows
High salinity, cold water and frequent flooding
Clear, fast-flowing water with no nutrients at all
High nutrient levels, warm water and low, slow river flows
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria grow fastest in warm, still water rich in phosphorus and nitrogen. Low flows from drought and extraction let the water warm and stratify. Fast, cold, turbulent flows mix the water and discourage blooms. Some blooms produce toxins that harm livestock and people.

questions.stem: How can extracting too much water from a river for irrigation affect the river's ecosystem downstream?
options: Lower flows always improve water quality by reducing sediment
Lower flows raise water levels in wetlands downstream
Lower flows only affect people, not the river's organisms
Lower flows reduce habitat and raise the risk of algal blooms
questions.explanation: Less water means shallower, warmer, slower river reaches and fewer floods to fill wetlands, so habitats shrink and breeding cues for fish and birds are lost. Low, warm flows also favour algal blooms and concentrate salts and pollutants.

questions.stem: Monitoring shows turbidity in a reservoir rose sharply after a bushfire burnt its catchment and heavy rain followed. Which explanation is best?
options: Ash in the air reduced rainfall, so the water became more concentrated
Algae died in the heat, so the water became clearer but more turbid
Bare soil eroded, washing sediment into the reservoir (siltation)
The fire heated the water, dissolving minerals from the reservoir floor
questions.explanation: With vegetation burnt off, heavy rain eroded the exposed soil and ash and carried them into the reservoir, raising turbidity and nutrient levels. Siltation also reduces storage capacity. This shows a natural process changing freshwater quality.

questions.stem: What is meant by the threshold of population viability?
options: The largest population an ecosystem can support at any time
The rate at which a population grows when resources are unlimited
The number of individuals that can be harvested each year
The smallest population size likely to persist in the long term
questions.explanation: Below a certain size, a population becomes likely to die out from chance events, inbreeding and difficulty finding mates. The largest supportable population is the carrying capacity, and the harvestable number is the sustainable yield.

questions.stem: Why is a population that falls below its viability threshold at risk even if the original threat is removed?
options: Small populations cannot be affected by disease or bushfire
The habitat automatically disappears once the population is small
Low genetic diversity and chance events can still wipe it out
Small populations always breed faster, so they quickly overshoot
questions.explanation: Very small populations lose genetic diversity through inbreeding and can be wiped out by a single fire, drought or disease outbreak. Finding mates may also be harder. These effects can keep pushing numbers down after the original cause is gone.

questions.stem: Clearing native vegetation for farming can cause dryland salinity. How can this push native populations below viability?
options: Salt from fertilisers is the only cause, so clearing has no effect
Salinity affects crops only, so native species are unaffected
Rising groundwater brings salt up, killing plants and habitat
Clearing lowers the water table, leaving salt deep underground
questions.explanation: Deep-rooted native plants use much of the rainfall. When they are replaced by shallow-rooted crops and pasture, more water reaches the groundwater, the water table rises and dissolved salts reach the root zone. Salt-sensitive vegetation dies, removing habitat for the species that depend on it.

questions.stem: Introduced foxes and cats prey on small native mammals in many parts of Australia. How can this affect ecosystem services as well as the mammals?
options: Losing small mammals has no effect, as they are not part of any food web
Losing animals that dig soil or spread seeds weakens soil and plant processes
Predators increase the number of native mammals by removing weak individuals
Introduced predators only affect cultural services, never supporting services
questions.explanation: Many small native mammals, such as bettongs and bandicoots, dig the soil, which helps water infiltration and nutrient cycling, and some spread fungal spores and seeds. Removing them reduces these supporting services. Pest predation can push already small populations below viability.

questions.stem: A forest is cut into small, isolated patches by roads and farms. The total forest area falls by 30%, but a forest-dwelling species declines far more. Which is the best explanation?
options: Fragmentation increases the total area of habitat available
Roads add food for the species, so its population overshoots
Isolated patches hold small populations that cannot mix or recolonise
The species needs exactly 70% of the original forest area to survive
questions.explanation: Habitat destruction and fragmentation leave separate small populations, each more likely to fall below viability through inbreeding and chance events. Animals may not cross gaps to find mates or recolonise empty patches, so the decline is greater than the area lost.

questions.stem: What is the maximum sustainable yield of a harvested population?
options: The total number of individuals in the population before harvesting began
The largest number that can be caught in a single year before the stock collapses
The yield when harvesting continues until no individuals remain
The largest harvest that can be taken each year without the population declining
questions.explanation: Maximum sustainable yield is the biggest catch that can be taken year after year while the population replaces its losses. A catch taken once, until the stock collapses, is not sustainable.

questions.stem: In a simple model of population growth, at what population size is the growth rate, and so the sustainable harvest, greatest?
options: Close to zero individuals
Twice the carrying capacity
About half the carrying capacity
Right at the carrying capacity
questions.explanation: A population grows slowly when very small, because there are few breeders, and slowly near carrying capacity, because resources are limiting. Growth is fastest in between, at about half the carrying capacity, so harvesting there gives the largest sustainable yield.

questions.stem: A fish stock has a carrying capacity of 10 000 tonnes, and its maximum sustainable yield is taken when the stock is near half that size. What happens if fishers keep taking that same annual catch after the stock has been reduced to 2000 tonnes?
options: The stock stays at 2000 tonnes, as the catch matches its growth
The stock grows past carrying capacity, as fewer fish compete
The catch exceeds the smaller stock's growth, so the stock falls further
The stock recovers, because smaller stocks grow faster than any others
questions.explanation: At 2000 tonnes the stock produces less new growth each year than it did at 5000 tonnes, so the same catch removes more than is replaced and the stock declines further. Sustainable catches must be reduced as stocks fall, which is why fisheries are monitored.

questions.stem: In a model, a population's yearly growth is r × N × (1 − N/K), with r = 0.4 per year and K = 10 000. What is the maximum sustainable yield, taken at N = 5000?
options: 2000 per year
4000 per year
500 per year
1000 per year
questions.explanation: At N = K/2 = 5000, growth = 0.4 × 5000 × (1 − 0.5) = 1000 per year, so 1000 can be harvested each year without decline. Forgetting the (1 − N/K) factor gives 2000, and using N = K gives zero growth.

questions.stem: Why do scientists who set fishing quotas need regular data on fish numbers, ages and breeding?
options: Data are needed only to set the market price of fish, not the catch
Stocks change, so the sustainable catch must be updated
Quotas are fixed forever once a fishery has first been opened
Fish numbers are always the same each year in every fishery
questions.explanation: Recruitment, predation and environmental conditions vary, so a catch that was sustainable one year may not be the next. Monitoring lets managers detect decline early and lower quotas before a stock falls below viability.

questions.stem: What does an ecological footprint measure?
options: The area of land that a city covers with its buildings, roads, parks and car parks
The number of species that are lost when land is cleared for development
The amount of carbon dioxide that one household emits each year from energy use
The productive land and water area needed to supply a population and absorb its wastes
questions.explanation: An ecological footprint converts the demand for food, timber, energy, space and waste absorption into the area of biologically productive land and water needed, usually in global hectares. It counts much more than built-up land, and more than carbon emissions alone.

questions.stem: A region's ecological footprint is 4.0 global hectares per person, but its biocapacity is only 1.6 global hectares per person. What does this show?
options: It uses 40% of what its own land and water can supply sustainably
It could support 2.4 times its present population sustainably
Its footprint and biocapacity are balanced, so its use is sustainable
It uses 2.5 times what its own land and water can supply sustainably
questions.explanation: 4.0 ÷ 1.6 = 2.5, so the region demands two and a half times its own biocapacity. The deficit is met by importing resources or by depleting stocks such as forests and fisheries. Dividing the other way gives 0.4, which inverts the comparison.

questions.stem: Which change would most reduce a household's ecological footprint?
options: Using less fossil fuel energy for transport and electricity
Moving to a much larger house on a bigger block of land
Buying more food that is flown in fresh from overseas
Replacing working appliances with new ones every year
questions.explanation: Energy from fossil fuels makes up a large part of most footprints, through the forest area needed to absorb the carbon dioxide. Larger homes, air-freighted food and frequent replacement of goods all increase the resources used and wastes produced.

questions.stem: Why does an ecological footprint include the area needed to absorb wastes, not just to produce resources?
options: Wastes are only produced by industry, so households can be excluded
Absorbing wastes uses no land, so it lowers the total footprint
Wastes are stored forever underground, so no ecosystem is involved
Absorbing wastes such as carbon dioxide also uses productive ecosystems
questions.explanation: Producing, transporting and processing resources all create wastes, and ecosystems such as forests and oceans are needed to absorb them. Counting this area shows the full demand that consumption places on Earth's renewable resources.
